nodes.summary: Given a bit string $w$, writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, the decoder reads a unary length prefix $1^n 0$ ($n$ ones followed by a zero) from the front of $w$, then reads exactly $n$ literals from the remaining bits with the literal decoder. The result is the clause made of these literals, in order, together with the bits left after them. Decoding fails if $w$ does not begin with such a prefix or one of the…
nodes.title: Decoding a length-prefixed clause

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$ and a bit string $w$, the decoder reads $n$ clauses one after another from the front of $w$ with the length-prefixed clause decoder. The result is the CNF formula made of these clauses, in order, together with the bits left after them; for $n = 0$ it is the empty formula together with $w$. Decoding fails if one of the $n$ clauses cannot be read.
nodes.title: Decoding a fixed number of clauses

nodes.summary: For every bit string $w$ and every CNF formula $\varphi$, the complete CNF decoder returns $\varphi$ on input $w$ if and only if $w$ is the length-prefixed binary code of $\varphi$.
nodes.title: The CNF decoder inverts the length-prefixed CNF code

nodes.summary: Given a bit string $w$, the decoder reads one CNF formula $\varphi$ from the front of $w$ with the length-prefixed CNF decoder, which also returns the bits left after $\varphi$. The result is $\varphi$ if no bits are left; decoding fails if no formula can be read or if bits remain after it.
nodes.title: Decoding a complete length-prefixed CNF formula

nodes.summary: Given a bit string $w$, writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, the decoder reads a unary length prefix $1^n 0$ ($n$ ones followed by a zero) from the front of $w$, then reads exactly $n$ clauses from the remaining bits with the length-prefixed clause decoder. The result is the CNF formula made of these clauses, in order, together with the bits left after them. Decoding fails if $w$ does not begin with such a…
nodes.title: Decoding a length-prefixed CNF formula

nodes.summary: Given a bit string $w$, the decoder reads a prefix-coded natural number $n$ from the front of $w$ and then one more bit $b$. The result is the literal $(n, b)$, with variable index $n$ and polarity $b$, together with the bits left after $b$. Decoding fails if no prefix-coded natural number can be read or no bit follows it.
nodes.title: Decoding a literal

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$ and a bit string $w$, the decoder reads $n$ literals one after another from the front of $w$ with the literal decoder. The result is the clause made of these literals, in order, together with the bits left after them; for $n = 0$ it is the empty clause together with $w$. Decoding fails if one of the $n$ literals cannot be read.
nodes.title: Decoding a fixed number of literals

nodes.summary: Given a bit string $w$, writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, the decoder reads one self-delimiting block $1\,b_1\,1\,b_2 \cdots 1\,b_k\,0$ from the front of $w$, with payload $b_1 \cdots b_k$ and remaining bits $r$. If the payload is the binary expansion of some natural number $n$, least significant bit first and without trailing zeros (empty for $n = 0$), the result is $(n, r)$. Decoding fails if $w$ does not…
nodes.title: Decoding a prefix-coded natural number

nodes.summary: Writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, the code of a clause $C = (\ell_1, \dots, \ell_k)$ is $1^k 0$ ($k$ ones followed by a zero) followed by the binary codes of $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_k$ in order, where a literal $(x, b)$ with variable index $x$ and polarity $b$ is coded by the prefix-free code of $x$ followed by the bit $b$.
nodes.title: Length-prefixed binary code of a clause

nodes.summary: Writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, the code of a CNF formula $\varphi = (C_1, \dots, C_m)$ is $1^m 0$ ($m$ ones followed by a zero) followed by the length-prefixed binary codes of the clauses $C_1, \dots, C_m$ in order.
nodes.title: Length-prefixed binary code of a CNF formula

nodes.summary: A literal $(n, b)$, with variable index $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and polarity $b \in \{\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true}\}$, is encoded as the prefix-free code of $n$ followed by the single bit $b$.
nodes.title: Binary code of a literal

nodes.summary: The code of $n \in \mathbb{N}$ is the self-delimiting block of the binary representation of $n$ (least significant bit first, with $0$ represented by the empty list): each bit $c$ is written as the two bits $\mathrm{true}, c$, and the block ends with a terminating $\mathrm{false}$.
nodes.title: Prefix-free code of a natural number

nodes.summary: A list $x$ of Booleans encodes a satisfiable CNF formula when $x$ is the binary code of some CNF formula $\varphi$ and $\varphi$ is satisfiable.
nodes.title: Encodings of satisfiable CNF formulas

nodes.summary: A decision problem $L_1$ reduces to a decision problem $L_2$ in polynomial time when there is a polynomial-time computable function $f$ from lists of Booleans to lists of Booleans such that $L_1(x) = L_2(f(x))$ for every list $x$ of Booleans.
nodes.title: Polynomial-time many-one reduction

nodes.summary: On a list of Booleans that begins with $k$ copies of $\mathrm{true}$ followed by $\mathrm{false}$, the reader returns $k$ together with the rest of the list after that $\mathrm{false}$. On a list containing no $\mathrm{false}$, including the empty list, it fails.
nodes.title: Reading a unary length prefix

nodes.summary: The SAT decision problem returns true on a list $x$ of Booleans when $x$ lies in the SAT language, that is, when $x$ encodes a satisfiable CNF formula, and false otherwise.
nodes.title: SAT as a decision problem

nodes.summary: SAT is the set of lists of Booleans that encode a satisfiable CNF formula.
nodes.title: The SAT language

nodes.summary: For all lists of Booleans $u$, $p$ and $r$, parsing one self-delimiting block from the front of $u$ succeeds with payload $p$ and remainder $r$ if and only if $u$ is the self-delimiting block of $p$ followed by $r$.
nodes.title: Parsing a self-delimiting block

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
